title: Your Ardas
hook: write the petition you'll bring to the Guru
tomorrow: what did the first Guru see when he looked up at the sky?

segments.voice: Yesterday, your hukam: the day's order, read from the top of the left-hand page and walked in. Now Simran has an assignment from her dad.

Simran's notes app has a page called my ardas, and so far it's a list. A good roommate. Passing chemistry. Not getting lost on a campus with too many buildings. Harjit wants the family to stand for an Ardas at home before she leaves, and Bebe told her to bring her own asking. So Simran pulls up the Ardas everyone stands for, to see where her list goes, and finds something odd. It barely asks for anything until near the end. It opens by remembering, name after name. And its very last line isn't about the person praying at all.
screen: `A LIST CALLED MY ARDAS.` → `IT OPENS BY REMEMBERING.` → `THE LAST LINE ISN'T ABOUT YOU.`

segments.voice: So where does she start? Where the Ardas does. Its opening comes from Guru Gobind Singh's Chandi di Var: in paraphrase, first remember the Divine, then Guru Nanak. Then the Gurus are named, one by one, all ten, and the Guru Granth Sahib. Then the Five Beloved, and the people who kept faith when it cost them everything. Only after all that remembering does the Ardas turn to asking, and there's a place there for what this family, this morning, needs. Here's the puzzle solved. By the time Simran reaches her list, she's standing at the end of a long line of people who carried the faith to her kitchen. Her roommate and her chemistry grade aren't too small for it. They just aren't alone anymore. Then the closing line: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhane sarbat da bhala. Through the Name, rising spirits; in your will, the good of all. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh standing prayer, after its personal asking, closes by asking good for everyone, strangers included. Simran adds one line to the bottom of her list. It isn't about her.
screen: `FIRST, REMEMBER.` · `THE GURUS, BY NAME.` · `THEN THE ASKING.` · `THE GOOD OF ALL.` · then, large: `MY ARDAS.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write one thing you'd bring to the Guru, in your own plain words, just as it is. Under it, write one line asking good for someone you'll never meet. Fold the paper and hold it while the sit runs.
Your Ardas: the standing petition, where your own asking finds its place after the remembering, and ends with the good of all.
Carry this: my ardas, my small asks inside a long line, closing with everyone. Written, folded, kept.

screen: `DAY 1780 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 20 OF 31.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DID THE FIRST GURU SEE IN THE SKY?`

howItsDone: Sikhs pray the Ardas standing, usually led by one person, at the close of services and before new beginnings such as a move, a trip or a wedding; the leader adds the particular petition of the day before the closing line.
